tasks.title: HTML parse on a cooperative task stack exhausts the stack and kills the process
tasks.evidence_before: Without any sanitizer: `swift test --filter AUDITDiagnosticsTests/testD_deepNestingThresholdWithoutASan` survives depth 1000 (clean malformedResponse) and DIES at depth 5000 with signal 10 (SIGBUS); `testE_deepNestingThroughHTMLExtraction` dies at depth 20000. With ASan the same failure appears at much lower depths and as a BUS in _platform_memset on a cooperative task (Task 3), which is how it was first found: `swift test --sanitize=address --filter ProviderContractTests/testDuckDuckGoTaxonomy` => signal 6. Attribution matrix: ScraperSupport.parse synchronously on the junk body = ok; DDG provider async on the same body = crash; DDG provider async on well-formed empty HTML = ok; TSan clean.
tasks.fix_summary: (1) MarkupDepth.containsMarkup rejects a body with no markup at all before parsing (ScraperSupport throws malformedResponse(provider)); scoped to the scrapers, because the web_open extractor must keep accepting plain text, JSON and YAML. (2) MarkupDepth.exceedsLimit counts element nesting iteratively on the raw bytes with an early exit and a cap of 512 (maximumNesting): comments, declarations, void elements, self-closing tags and raw-text element content (script/style/...) open no level, a '>' in a quoted attribute does not end a tag, a stray '<' is text. Exceeding it throws the new SearchError.markupDepthExceeded(limit), category .malformedResponse. (3) LargeStackParse.run executes the recursive part of ScraperSupport.parse and HTMLExtractor.extract on a dedicated 8 MiB-stack thread, synchronously, publishing the outcome through a Sendable OSAllocatedUnfairLock (no @unchecked Sendable, no unsynchronised shared state, deadlock-free because the parse thread does no Swift concurrency work). (4) Tests/WebSearchCoreTests/MarkupDepthTests.swift: 19 tests, including the three original probe inputs as assertions and a 512-deep document parsed via Task.detached; the temporary AUDITDiagnosticsTests.swift probes were deleted in the same commit. No byte cap added: the measured inputs are 25 KB and 100 KB, so size does not bound depth.
tasks.evidence_after: swift test --sanitize=address --filter 'MarkupDepthTests|ProviderContractTests|HTMLExtractorTests' => 81 tests, 0 failures, exit 0 (the run that previously ended in AddressSanitizer: BUS), including a 512-deep document parsed on a cooperative task. swift test --filter 'MarkupDepthTests|HTMLExtractorTests|FetchFallbackTests|FetchBehaviorTests' => 45 tests, 0 failures. Full suite swift test => 390 tests, 6 skipped, 0 failures (baseline 371/6, so +19 regression tests). swift build and swift build -c release => 0 warnings, 0 errors (baseline 0). Artifact: AUDIT/evidence/A01-asan.txt. Removing either the depth guard or the large-stack hop makes MarkupDepthTests kill the runner again (SIGBUS / signal 4).
tasks.notes: Reachability: web_open parses arbitrary attacker-controlled pages; the scraper path is opt-in but enabled in some deployments. Depth 5000 is ~25 KB of markup, 20000 is ~100 KB, both far below the 4 MiB response cap, so size limits do not bound depth; body size is capped where bodies are read. Item (3) of the fix was promoted from belt-and-braces to load-bearing by measurement: with the depth cap alone, a document AT the cap still overflowed a cooperative task stack under AddressSanitizer. Rather than lower the cap until the instrument was satisfied (which would make a production parameter depend on a debug build), the parse got a stack with room for the bound.

tasks.title: The HTTP transport serves exactly one MCP session per process, and that session can never be released

tasks.evidence_before:
`authorize` splits on the *snapshot* state taken one `await` earlier:

  ```swift

      let allowed = await breaker.shouldAttempt()
      if !allowed { return ProviderFailure(..., category: .circuitOpen, ...) }
  } else {
      _ = await breaker.shouldAttempt()          // ← refusal discarded
  }
  ```

  `CircuitBreaker.shouldAttempt()` is the thing that owns the invariant — its own doc comment
  says "*A half-open probe is claimed by the first caller only, so a burst of concurrent
  searches cannot all hammer a recovering provider*" (`CircuitBreaker.swift:71-74`) — and it

  concurrent fan-out of *every* in-flight search, which is exactly the load that re-opened its

  a CSI sequence except `ESC` a width of 1 — while its sibling `displayWidth`
  (`Terminal.swift:116-136`) skips escape sequences entirely and is documented as the width
  contract ("*Counts ANSI escape sequences as zero width, which matters because styled text is
  padded after colouring*"). The two disagree, so `Renderer` can (and at narrow widths does)
  cut a styled line inside a colour run and return it without the `\u{1B}[0m` that closes it;
  the colour then bleeds into the following columns and lines. Worked example with the exact
  algorithm: `truncate("\u{1B}[91m" + 40 × "x" + "\u{1B}[0m", to: 10)` consumes
  `ESC [ 9 1 m` (4 counted units) plus 5 `x`, then stops at the limit — the result is
  `"\u{1B}[91mxxxxx…"` with **no reset**, so everything after it is red. Cuts *inside* a
  sequence are equally reachable at other widths (stopping after `\u{1B}[9` leaves an
  unterminated CSI). No test covers styled truncation: `TerminalLayoutTests` truncates plain
  text only, and `testNoLineExceedsTerminalWidth` asserts only `displayWidth`, which passes
  with a dropped reset.

tasks.title: The response-level resale discount is applied to every result of an aggregator response, defeating the per-result refinement the code documents
tasks.discovered_by: handover re-read L2 (independent re-read of RankFusion against its own documented intent)
tasks.evidence_before:
`RankFusion.fuse` decides the aggregator discount per result but ORs the response-level flag into it:

```swift
// RankFusion.swift:115-117  (the documented intent)
// Reservations are decided per result as well as per response: an instance can
// serve one page from Brave and another from Google, and only the resold one
// should lose the aggregator vote.
let responseResellsOwnedIndex = RankFusion.resellsIndexAlreadyOwned(
    response: response, ownedFamilies: ownedFamilies)
```
```swift
// RankFusion.swift:157-164  (what actually happens)
rawWeight: weight(
    for: contributionFamily, provider: provider, base: base,
    duplicatedOwnedIndex: responseResellsOwnedIndex || resoldFamily != nil,
    configuration: configuration)
```

`resellsIndexAlreadyOwned` (`:277-290`) scans the **response-level** `upstreamEngines`, so one resold
engine anywhere in a multi-engine response discounts **every** result in that response - including
results whose own per-result `upstreamEngines` name an index nobody else owns. It also omits the
`family.isIndependentIndex` guard that `resoldFamily` (`:305-311`) applies, so a response-level hit on
a non-independent family (Google, DuckDuckGo) discounts results that the per-result test would never
touch. `response.upstreamEngines` is populated by the aggregator adapters (`SearXNGProvider.swift:107-111,153`,
`OpenWebSearchProvider.swift:116-120,157`), so this is reachable whenever a local SearXNG instance
resells Brave beside a page it took from somewhere we do not own.
tasks.notes: expected-correct: when a result carries its own per-result engine attribution, the discount decision must be per-result only (`resoldFamily != nil`); the response-level flag is the fallback for adapters that report engines only at the response level, so it must apply only where `result.upstreamEngines` is nil. Give `resellsIndexAlreadyOwned` the same `isIndependentIndex` guard `resoldFamily` has, or derive a single decision function that both call. Add a fusion test with one response holding two results - one from an owned index, one from an unowned one - and assert only the first loses the aggregator weight. · confidence: certain

tasks.title: Nullable enum arguments declare `["string", "null"]` with an `enum` that excludes `null`, so a strict client filling every `required` slot cannot legally send the null the design depends on
tasks.discovered_by: handover re-read L1 (JSON Schema conjunction re-check of the nullable-enum arguments)
tasks.evidence_before:
Every optional argument in this file is expressed as a nullable union with all properties listed in
`required` - that is the documented strict-mode idiom (`ToolSchemas.swift:19-33`) - and the runtime
parser treats an explicit null as absent (`ToolArguments.string`, `:438-444`: `.null` -> `nil`).
But where the argument also carries an `enum`, the enum does not admit null:

```swift
// ToolSchemas.swift:62-66
"recency": [
    "type": ["string", "null"],
    "enum": ["any", "day", "week", "month", "year"],
    …
],
```

In JSON Schema `type` and `enum` are conjunctive, so `null` satisfies `type` and violates `enum`:
the value is invalid. Affected: `web_search.recency` (`:62-66`), `.provider` (`:83-93`), `.mode`
(`:94-101`) and `web_answer.mode` (`:270-274`). A strict consumer that must supply every `required`
property therefore cannot legally express "use the default" for any of them. The repository's own
lint does not catch it because `SchemaCompatibilityTests` asserts nullability from `type` alone
(`SchemaCompatibilityTests.swift:275-296`), never against `enum`.
tasks.notes: expected-correct: either add `null` to each such `enum` (`"enum": ["any", "day", "week", "month", "year", null]`) so the union is expressible, or drop these from `required` and document the omission. Extend the schema lint to assert that for every property whose `type` includes `"null"`, a null value validates - that check is what would have caught this. · confidence: certain on the contradiction; the client-visible impact is unverified because no vendor client is run (see the Compatibility bound).

tasks.title: The HTTP smoke picks a free port by closing the socket before the child binds, so the child can lose the bind race
tasks.discovered_by: Phase C (the residual B83 deliberately left in place)
tasks.evidence_before:
`free_loopback_port()` binds port 0, reads the assigned port, closes the socket and returns the
number; `run_http_smoke` then starts the child with that port. Between the close and the child's
own bind the port is unowned, so another process can take it and the child exits with
`EADDRINUSE`. B83 fixed the *symptom* - the wait loop now polls the child and reports the exit
code with its stderr in under a second instead of spinning the full 20 s and blaming the port -
but the race itself remains, and this is the same class of defect B20 fixed in the Swift
HTTP-transport harness.
tasks.notes:
expected-correct: make the child's bind authoritative rather than pre-emptive. Either have the
child report the port it actually bound (the server already writes diagnostics to stderr, so a
chosen-port line is the natural handshake), or classify a bind failure and retry once on a fresh
port. Holding the parent socket open across the exec is not a fix: macOS `SO_REUSEADDR` does not
permit two live binders, so the child would still fail. · confidence: certain on the race; the
handshake design is the author's call.

tasks.title: A local throttle that cleared between the authorise and the wait estimate was reported as a hard skip, making the suite intermittently red
tasks.discovered_by: Phase E baseline (the suite failed about 1 run in 20 on the independent host)
tasks.evidence_before:
`StdioServerTests.testToolArgumentClampsAreEnforced` failed about once in twenty runs at
`XCTUnwrap` on the second `web_search`'s structured results. Reproduced deterministically by
reading the code:

```swift
// authorizationAfterBoundedWait, before
guard allowWaiting, denial.category == .rateLimited,
    let wait = await health.localWait(for: id),
    wait <= SearchOrchestrator.maximumLocalWait,
    wait.milliseconds <= Int(Double(budget.milliseconds) * localWaitBudgetShare)
else { return denial }
```

`authorize` denies because `elapsed` is just under the limiter's `minimumInterval`; a few
microseconds later `localWait` re-reads the clock and correctly reports "available now" by
returning **nil** (`RateLimiter.timeUntilAvailable` returns nil when a token is available now).
The combined guard reads that nil as "cannot wait" and returns the stale denial, so the
provider is recorded `skippedLocally`, nothing is returned, and with a single provider the tool
call becomes an error with no structured content - exactly the observed failure. Separately,
the same function's minimum-interval branch truncated (`Int(remaining * 1000)`) while the token
branch below it used `.rounded(.up)`, so an estimate could be up to a millisecond short, or
`.milliseconds(0)` for a sub-millisecond remainder; a caller sleeping a truncated estimate can
wake a hair early and be denied again by the single retry.
tasks.fix_summary: Two changes. authorizationAfterBoundedWait now treats a nil wait estimate from a locally rate-limited provider as 'the throttle has already cleared' and retries authorize, instead of discarding the stale denial; only a non-nil estimate beyond the caps gives up. And RateLimiter.timeUntilAvailable rounds the minimum-interval remainder UP (matching the token branch below it) and returns nil rather than .milliseconds(0) when the remainder rounds to zero, so a caller that sleeps exactly what it was told cannot wake early and be denied again.
tasks.evidence_after: Before: the suite was intermittently red on this host - testToolArgumentClampsAreEnforced failed about once in twenty runs with XCTUnwrap on the second web_search's structured results. Root cause: authorize denies because elapsed is just under the limiter's minimumInterval, then localWait re-reads the clock a few microseconds later and correctly reports 'available now' by returning nil, which the combined guard treated as 'cannot wait' and returned the stale denial, losing a search that had a usable provider (and with a single provider, the whole tool call). The token branch already rounded up; the min-interval branch truncated, which could also return .milliseconds(0). After: three deterministic tests, including a purpose-built CreepingClock that advances 1 ms on every now() read so the two reads straddle the boundary on every run. Mutation-proven: reverting the orchestrator arm gives 'temporarilyUnavailable([...tavily, ...rateLimited, message: "Tavily is locally rate limited.")]' (the exact diagnosed skip), and reverting the rounding gives XCTAssertGreaterThanOrEqual failed ("0.0") is less than ("0.0005") plus XCTAssertGreaterThan failed ("0") is not greater than ("0"). Gates: debug and release build with 0 warnings under -warnings-as-errors; 489 tests / 6 skipped / 0 failures (486 baseline + 3 new); swift-format --strict 0; swiftlint --strict 0 in 84 files. 33 consecutive full-suite runs green, though the deterministic mutation is the real proof - 32 clean runs of a 1-in-20 flake is only about 81% confidence. Artifact: AUDIT/evidence/B116-local-throttle-race.txt

expected-correct: treat a nil wait estimate from a locally rate-limited provider as "the
